messages.text: Family of 5 here, combined income around $4,150 a month. Worth applying for food stamps?

**Yes, it's worth applying.** Your income looks close to the line, but it may be under it. Only the Tennessee Department of Human Services (TDHS) can decide.

**What I found**
- A search of USDA's 2026–27 income table gave a limit of about **$4,191 a month before taxes** for a family of 5. I couldn't open the USDA page myself, so please treat that number as unconfirmed. [USDA 2026–27 table](https://www.usda.gov/sites/default/files/guidance-documents/fna.snap-cola2027.pdf)
- If $4,150 is your income before taxes, you'd be just under that limit. That means food assistance (SNAP) is **possible**.
- Tennessee's income limit is unsettled. The official federal limit is 130% of poverty. Some sources report a higher state limit. TDHS has also proposed changing its rules, but that needs approval from the state legislature. [Sycamore Institute](https://sycamoretn.org/snap-in-tn/)
- Because of that, I can't say for sure which limit applies. Applying is the best way to find out.
- The Sycamore Institute page says most households can have up to $3,000 in savings. It's $4,500 if someone is 60+ or has a disability.

**How to apply** ([TDHS SNAP page](https://www.tn.gov/humanservices/for-families/supplemental-nutrition-assistance-program-snap.html))
- Online: onedhs.tn.gov/csp, open 24/7
- Phone: 1-833-772-8347 (TTY: 711)
- You can also call 211 for free local help.
- Having proof of income, rent, and utility bills ready can speed things up.

**Two questions so I can estimate your monthly amount**
1. Is the $4,150 your income **before taxes**, and does it all come from jobs? Or is some of it Social Security, unemployment, or child support?
2. How much do you pay each month for rent or mortgage? Do you pay heating or cooling bills separately?

I can also check WIC and TennCare/CoverKids if you have kids under 5, or if anyone is pregnant.

Yes, $4,150 is before taxes and it all comes from our jobs, both of us. No Social Security, unemployment, or child support.

Rent is $1,400. We pay heating/cooling separately, but I'm not sure exactly what it runs each month since it changes.

Thanks, that helps. SNAP looks **possible** for your family. My rough guess is **$300 to $400 a month**, but that is only an estimate. TDHS will work out the real amount.

**How I got that estimate**
- Your income before taxes is $4,150. That's just under the $4,191 limit I found for a family of 5. I couldn't open USDA's page to confirm it, so treat it as unconfirmed. [USDA 2026–27 table](https://www.usda.gov/sites/default/files/guidance-documents/fna.snap-cola2027.pdf)
- SNAP takes some money off your income first. That includes 20% of work pay, a standard amount for a family your size, and part of your housing and utility costs.
- After those, your countable income comes to roughly $2,800 to $3,050 a month. The limit for that step is about $3,224, so you'd be under it. This limit is also unconfirmed.
- I used a top benefit of about $1,217 for 5 people. Search results showed that figure, but I couldn't open the USDA page to confirm it.
- I couldn't find Tennessee's set amount for heating and cooling bills. It's a flat allowance, so you don't need to know your exact bills. I tried a few possible amounts, and that's why my estimate is a range.

**Things to know**
- Tennessee's income limit is unsettled. The official federal limit is 130% of poverty, but some sources report a higher state limit. TDHS has also proposed rule changes that need legislative approval. This is another reason to apply. [Sycamore Institute](https://sycamoretn.org/snap-in-tn/)
- Most households can have up to $3,000 in savings. It's $4,500 if someone is 60+ or has a disability. [Sycamore Institute](https://sycamoretn.org/snap-in-tn/)
- Child care costs, and medical bills for anyone 60+ or with a disability, could raise your amount.

**Next steps** ([TDHS SNAP page](https://www.tn.gov/humanservices/for-families/supplemental-nutrition-assistance-program-snap.html))
- Apply online at onedhs.tn.gov/csp, or call 1-833-772-8347 (TTY: 711).
- You can also call 211 for free local help.
- Have proof of income, rent, and utility bills ready.
- Only TDHS decides. Please report your income and household accurately, because overpayments have to be paid back.

**Two more questions**
1. Do you pay for child care so you can work? If so, about how much a month?
2. How old are your kids? Is anyone pregnant or breastfeeding? I can check WIC and TennCare/CoverKids too.
No child care, we don't pay for any. Kids are 15, 11 and 7. Nobody's pregnant or breastfeeding.

**WIC:** WIC looks **unlikely** for your family. It's for pregnant or breastfeeding women, babies, and children under 5. Your kids are 15, 11, and 7, so none of them are in that group.

**CoverKids / TennCare for your kids:** This looks **likely**.
- Tennessee covers children under 19 through TennCare or CoverKids. CoverKids is for kids who don't qualify for TennCare but whose family income is at or below about 250% of the poverty level.
- For a family of 5, searches showed a limit of roughly **$8,000 a month** before taxes. I couldn't open the state's own chart to confirm it, so treat that number as unconfirmed. [Search result: Tennessee's CoverKids eligibility guide](https://www.tn.gov/coverkids/coverkids/redirect-income-guidelines.html)
- Your $4,150 a month is well under that.
- I don't have a confirmed figure for the parents. TennCare is much stricter for adults, so a caseworker would need to look at that.

**SNAP:** This still looks **possible**, with an estimate of about **$300 to $400 a month**. With no child care costs, I can't add anything to that estimate. The Tennessee income limit is still unsettled, so applying is the best way to find out. [Sycamore Institute](https://sycamoretn.org/snap-in-tn/)

**Next steps**
- **SNAP:** onedhs.tn.gov/csp or 1-833-772-8347 (TTY: 711). [TDHS SNAP page](https://www.tn.gov/humanservices/for-families/supplemental-nutrition-assistance-program-snap.html)
- **TennCare/CoverKids:** Apply at tenncareconnect.tn.gov. I couldn't open the state's page to confirm the phone number, so please check it there. Or call 211 and they'll point you to the right line.
- 211 can also give you free help with the applications.
- Only the state agencies decide. Please list your income and household accurately, because overpayments have to be paid back.

If your family has a disability, or anyone is 60 or older, tell me. Medical bills could raise your SNAP amount.

The USDA's official FY2027 table gives a gross monthly income limit of **$4,191** for a five-person household in the 48 states, D.C., Guam, and the Virgin Islands. That is 130% of the poverty level, effective October 1, 2026 through September 30, 2027. Alaska's limit is $5,238 and Hawaii's is $4,819 ([USDA FY2027 income standards PDF](https://www.usda.gov/sites/default/files/guidance-documents/fna.snap-cola2027.pdf)).

Other five-person figures from the same USDA table:
- **Net monthly income limit (100% of poverty level):** $3,224 in the 48 states and D.C., $4,030 in Alaska, and $3,707 in Hawaii.
- **Elderly or disabled households that form a separate household (165% of poverty level):** $5,319 in the 48 states and D.C.

For comparison, the FY2026 gross limit for five people was $4,079 ([North Dakota SNAP policy manual](https://www.nd.gov/dhs/policymanuals/SNAP/Content/Policy%20Update%20Documentation/2026/SNAP%20Release%2026.3%20Effective%204.1.2026.pdf)), so the FY2027 figure is higher.

States using broad-based categorical eligibility can set higher gross limits. For example, one state's chart shows a 200%-of-poverty standard for that policy ([Louisiana DCFS chart](https://public.powerdms.com/LADCFS/documents/399088)). Check the rules of the state where the household applies.

I didn't find an official TDHS figure for a household of 5. The sources I found are mostly unofficial and disagree with each other.

- **Gross income:** Most sources say the gross monthly limit is 130% of the federal poverty level. For a household of 5, the figures range widely, from about $3,161 in one source to $3,807 in another. One listing puts it at $3,197, and another at $3,201.
- **Net income:** One source says the net limit is 100% of the poverty level, which it lists as $2,455 for five people. That source also notes that deductions can be made from the gross income to reach the net income.
- **Recent changes:** Sycamore Institute's SNAP page, which is the most credible source I found, gives a family-of-four gross limit of $3,483. It also says that pending approval from the Tennessee General Assembly, TDHS is in the process of changing state-level "broad-based categorical eligibility" (BBCE) rules, which could change the income limits.
- **Resources:** One source lists a resource limit of $2,250 or less, but the sources don't agree on this either.

The most reliable approach is to check the current income chart on the Tennessee Department of Human Services website, since the sources here predate or misstate the current figures. I'd treat the household-of-5 numbers above as unverified.

input.prompt: What are Tennessee SNAP income limits, broad-based categorical eligibility status (130% vs 200%), and any recent changes? Household of 5 figures.

tool_calls.result:
**Income limits (family of four; the article gives no figures for a household of five)**
- **Gross monthly income:** 130% of the poverty line, or $3,483. This counts all income before deductions.
- **Net monthly income:** 100% of the poverty line, or $2,680.
- **Resource limit:** $3,000 for most households, or $4,500 if a member has a disability or is age 60+.

**Household of 5:** The article doesn't state limits for five-person households, so I can't give those figures.

**BBCE (130% vs. 200%):** The article doesn't mention a 200% threshold. It describes the current federal gross income test at 130% of poverty. It also says TDHS is changing state-level broad-based categorical eligibility rules to align SNAP income limits with TANF, but that change requires General Assembly approval. The article doesn't give the proposed thresholds, so I can't confirm whether 200% applies.

**Recent changes:**
- **BBCE:** TDHS has proposed changing state BBCE rules, pending legislative approval.
- **Work requirements (One Big Beautiful Bill Act):** The ABAWD requirement now applies to ages 18–64 without a dependent under 14, up from 18–54 without a dependent under 18. Exemptions for veterans, people experiencing homelessness, and former foster youth ages 24+ were removed. The article projects about 52,000 Tennesseans will now have to meet it.
- **Administrative costs:** The state's share rises from 50% to 75% starting October 1, 2026. TDHS estimates it needs an additional $77 million in recurring state funds.
- **Benefit cost-sharing:** Starting October 2027, states with payment error rates above 6% may have to cover up to 15% of benefit costs. Tennessee's FY 2024 rate was 9.5%, which could mean $81–243 million in state costs.

I couldn't find the official tn.gov or onedhs.tn.gov SNAP income chart in these results. Every source is a third-party site, and they disagree on the numbers. The federal FY2026 figures (October 1, 2025 to September 30, 2026) are the most consistent across them, so verify against the state before relying on any of them.

- **Gross limit (130% FPL):** Most sources put the 4-person limit at about $3,483/month. Others give $3,575, $3,482, $3,380, or $3,250. The 1-person limit is usually about $1,696 and the 2-person limit about $2,292. The 1-person gross limit is $1,696 and the 4-person limit is $3,483 per month.
- **Net limit (100% FPL):** The 4-person figure is most often $2,680, though one source gives $2,750. The 1-person net limit is about $1,305.
- **Maximum benefit:** Most sources list $298 for one person and $994 for four. One source gives $975 for four.
- **Broad-based categorical eligibility (BBCE):** Sources conflict. One says Tennessee applies the federal default gross-income limit of 130% of the Federal Poverty Level — no BBCE in this jurisdiction. Another describes a higher BBCE gross limit, $2,608 for one person, alongside the standard test. I could not confirm which is correct from these results.
- **Timing:** One source notes that the figures above stay in effect until new numbers are published, typically around October 1, 2026. Today is October 22, 2026, so FY2027 figures may already be out on tn.gov even though they weren't in these results.

A follow-up search for the tn.gov SNAP page or a USDA FY2027 COLA memo would resolve the discrepancies.
